source.title_on_document: Empowering Engineering Students Through Artificial Intelligence (AI): Blended Human–AI Creative Ideation Processes With ChatGPT

supplement.where: No supplementary material or appendix is cited in the document. The PDF ends with references on pp. 17–19.
supplement.holds: Not stated. Exact numerical results for the randomized assistance comparison are absent from the PDF; no external supplement containing them is identified.

paper_design_summary: In a supervised classroom crossover experiment, 51 third-year industrial-design engineering students were randomly assigned to opposite orders of ChatGPT-assisted and unaided ideation, first improving public transport and then university spaces (pp. 4, 6–7). They produced sketches and brief descriptions; student peers subsequently assessed 728 ideas on creativity, innovation, viability, user benefits, value, complexity and overall quality, while a survey captured the same participants' perceptions (pp. 5–9, 14). The second-task unaided outputs were produced after AI removal, and the paper separately compared assisted ideas by nonrandomized prior ChatGPT experience (pp. 7, 9, 11).

studies.label: Randomized classroom crossover: public-transport and university-space ideation

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were randomly assigned to Group A or Group B. Group A worked without ChatGPT on Task 1 and with ChatGPT on Task 2; Group B had the reverse assistance order. Task topics remained in fixed order. Group roles and classrooms switched after Task 1. Individual assignment to these groups randomized within-person assistance order; the randomization mechanism and sequence-group sizes are not stated.
assignment.quote: For the experiment, students were randomly assigned to two groups and placed in classrooms based on their respective group assignments:

assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration or registration reference is stated in the document.

arms.name: With ChatGPT
arms.description: Assisted crossover condition: Group B on Task 1 and Group A on Task 2. Supervised use of ChatGPT on university-supplied computers; other websites and tools were restricted. Condition and sequence-group participant counts are not separately printed (pp. 6–7, Section 4.3.1 and Figure 1).

arms.name: Without ChatGPT
arms.description: Unaided crossover condition: Group A on Task 1 and Group B on Task 2, in a supervised computer-free classroom without external support tools. Group B's Task 2 ideas were produced after its earlier AI use; this condition therefore mixes pre-exposure and after-AI output in the pooled results (pp. 6–7, Section 4.3.1 and Figure 1). Condition and sequence-group participant counts are not separately printed.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or attrition are described. The paper identifies 51 participants and later explicitly links its results and the generated ideas to that cohort, but does not give a separate count at random assignment or counts for the two sequence groups (p. 4, Section 4.1; p. 16, Section 7). Table 4's n = 80 and n = 280 are idea counts, not people (p. 11).
participants.who: Third-year undergraduate students in Engineering specializing in Industrial Design and Product Development at Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya · BarcelonaTech (UPC). They generated the ideas and later assessed peers' ideas; the evaluation session is not a second independent participant sample (pp. 4, 8, 16).
participants.country: Spain (study institution; p. 1 affiliations and p. 4, Section 4.1). Participant nationality is not stated.
participants.quote: The results of this research primarily derive from a cohort of 51 engineering students specializing in Industrial Design and Product Development.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 4.1; p. 16, Section 7 (cohort contributing results and peer evaluation)

ai_tool.how_used: Students used the text chatbot for questions, explanations, ideation directions and background information while creating their own sketches and descriptions. They were instructed to use ChatGPT in the assisted condition; other tools and external websites were restricted. No standardized prompt, prior training intervention or image generation was described (pp. 6–7, Section 4.3.1).

task.description: Generate innovative ideas to improve public transport (Task 1) and university spaces (Task 2). Each idea was submitted as a sketch and a brief written description on an A5 template, with instructions to produce eight unique ideas per task. These are design-ideation outputs, not model-only responses (pp. 6–8, Section 4.3.1 and Figures 2–3).
task.duration: 30 min per task; conditions and classrooms reversed after Task 1 (pp. 6–7, Section 4.3.1).

outcomes.name: Creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three items assess creativity, original problem solving and unconventionality. Peer assessments use a 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 4 (Strongly Agree) scale (p. 5, Table 1 and Section 4.2.1). Student peers rated anonymous ideas and could not rate their own contributions (p. 8, Section 4.3.2). Figure 7 reports Task 1, Task 2 and Total as panels of the same outcome; Table 4 reports an observational previous-experience subgroup comparison. The 728 units are the full peer-assessed idea corpus (p. 14, Discussion, Research question 2); Table 4 has its own printed idea counts. AI availability here describes the assisted side of the comparison. The Task 2 unaided control was produced after AI removal (p. 7, Figure 1); see notes.
outcomes.delay: Ideas were produced in the first experimental session and rated in a second session; the interval between sessions is not stated (pp. 6–8, Section 4.3). The later rating session is not a delayed creative-production task.

contrasts.reported: The paper reports no significant Mann–Whitney difference between AI-assisted and unaided ideas. Figure 7 presents Task 1, Task 2 and Total on a 1–4 scale, with bars and error bars but without numerical data labels. Exact arm means, SDs, SEs, test statistics and p values for this assistance comparison are not printed, and the error bars are not defined. Task 2 compares currently assisted Group A with Group B working without AI after its Task 1 exposure; the pooled comparison therefore includes an after-AI control.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 5 (peer-evaluation results); p. 11, Figure 7; p. 14, Discussion, Research question 2; p. 7, Figure 1 for crossover timing

outcomes.name: Number of ideas generated (descriptive totals)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Counts of submitted ideas, reported only as task-by-condition totals, not as participant-level fluency means or an inferential fluency analysis. Participants were instructed to generate eight unique ideas per task (p. 6, Section 4.3.1). Unit is set because Table 3 summarizes condition-level pools; the number of independent set observations is not explicitly reported, so n_units is null. The paper's 728 is the total number of ideas, not the number of people or sets. The Task 2 control pool was produced after AI removal (p. 7, Figure 1).
outcomes.delay: Both ideation tasks occurred during the first experimental session (pp. 6–7, Section 4.3.1).

contrasts.reported: Table 3: Control group—Task 1 158, Task 2 202, Subtotal 360; Experimental group—Task 1 195, Task 2 173, Subtotal 368; Subtotal—Task 1 353, Task 2 375, total 728. These are idea counts. Figure 1 identifies Control as without ChatGPT and Experimental as with ChatGPT in each task, with the students crossing over. AI-assisted totals are higher in Task 1 and lower in Task 2. No participant-level means, SDs or statistical test for fluency are reported.

eligibility.reason: Random allocation of students to opposite AI-assistance orders is explicit (p. 6, Section 4.3.1; p. 7, Figure 1). The analyzed study cohort is 51 people, just above the 50-person threshold, as supported by the participant description and the limitations discussion linking that cohort to the results; 728 refers to ideas (p. 4, Section 4.1; p. 16, Section 7; p. 7, Table 3). Student peers evaluated actual ideas, including creativity, using an output-rating instrument (p. 5, Table 1; p. 8, Section 4.3.2; p. 14, Discussion, Research question 2). The first-task randomized assistance contrast meets the criteria independently of the second-task after-AI control issue. Core inclusion does not establish availability of a usable effect estimate or participant-level precision.

one_line_finding: Among 51 students producing 728 ideas, ChatGPT assistance yielded no significant peer-rated differences, while prior ChatGPT users' assisted ideas had higher overall scores than novices' (3.00 [SD 0.82] versus 2.75 [SD 0.94], p = 0.039; p. 4, Section 4.1; p. 7, Table 3; p. 9, Results; p. 11, Figure 7 and Table 4).
open_questions: What are the participant counts at randomization and in each crossover sequence, and were any participants or idea ratings excluded? The document gives a 51-person study cohort but no allocation-specific or attrition counts (pp. 4, 6–9, 16).

Can exact task-specific and pooled AI-versus-unaided means, SDs, test statistics and p values be obtained, together with the definition of Figure 7's error bars? These are not printed (pp. 9, 11, 14).
Why do the previous-experience idea counts in Table 4 (NPE n = 80; PE n = 280) not reconcile with the 368 assisted ideas in Table 3? No exclusion or reconciliation is provided (pp. 7, 11).

Can an analysis account for multiple ideas per person, the randomized crossover order, task differences and possible carryover? The described Mann–Whitney analyses do not state participant clustering or paired-person treatment (pp. 8–9, Section 4.4; p. 11, Table 4).

How should the Task 2 unaided series be used for after_ai evidence? Group B produced it after AI removal, but the contemporaneous Group A comparison had AI available, and no separate unassisted post-exposure versus unexposed comparison is reported (p. 7, Figure 1; p. 11, Figure 7).
notes:
Read all 19 PDF pages and the entire markdown conversion, including the reference list; no appendix is present. Outcome inventory: Table 1 and Figure 7 contain seven peer-rated idea qualities (creativity, innovation, viability, user benefits, value, complexity and overall score); Table 3 contains descriptive idea totals; Table 4 repeats the same seven rating outcomes by prior experience. These yield eight distinct output-outcome families, with task panels and subgroup analyses retained within each family rather than counted as additional studies or measures. Table 2 and Figures 4–6 report previous use, general impressions, perceived idea qualities, experience and efficiency; Figure 8 and Table 5 report qualitative advantages, drawbacks, tips and threats. These self-reports are excluded from the output-outcome list. Homogeneity in Table 5 (p. 14) is a perceived threat, not measured diversity across participants' outputs.

Timing: Figure 1 (p. 7) shows Group A unaided then assisted, and Group B assisted then unaided. Group B's Task 2 unaided output series is after_ai: AI was removed before those ideas were produced. The with_ai coding above applies to the paper's assistance contrasts and the currently assisted side, not to that post-exposure control series. Figure 7's pooled comparison mixes pre-exposure and post-exposure unaided controls. No separate after_ai effect is created from comparing different tasks or treating the other group's currently assisted Task 2 work as an unexposed unaided control. The second evaluation session scored already-produced ideas; it is not a new unassisted creativity test (pp. 6–8).

Design is coded lab_rct because the reported intervention is a supervised, controlled classroom session, with random assignment to assistance order; the paper does not explicitly identify it as ordinary coursework or a named course intervention (pp. 4, 6–8). Peer raters are students, not the experts who reviewed the instrument (pp. 5, 8, 16). The separate prior-experience comparison is observational within the same sample and is labeled other, not ai_design or randomized AI-versus-no-AI. Its r values are printed rank-test effects; no effect sizes have been computed. Table 4's printed idea counts and signs, including the negative z for viability, are retained unchanged.

Numerical verification: Table 3 and Table 4 were checked against their PDF pages; Figure 7 was visually inspected. No graph values or error bars were digitized or estimated. The full corpus count for the seven rating outcomes is supported by the statement that the 728 generated ideas were peer-assessed (p. 14). Table 4's subgroup counts are separate and unreconciled. The reported method does not establish participant-level standard errors; core eligibility should not be read as readiness for pooling (pp. 8–9, 11).

No primary outcome is explicitly designated and no preregistration is stated. No public data or code URL is given; the Data Availability Statement says data and materials are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request (p. 17). No external source or another screener's form was used.

The Results section also states that previous-experience groups did not differ significantly when working without ChatGPT, but supplies no numerical statistics for that unaided subgroup comparison (p. 9).
